answers: A group is a maximal contiguous balanced parenthesis substring: it begins where the depth goes from 0 to 1 and ends where the depth returns to 0. Parentheses nested inside that span belong to the same single group, not to separate groups.

The list should include every possible prefix of the string, from length 1 up through the full string length, ordered shortest to longest (and includes the empty-string case only insofar as the string itself is non-empty -- for an empty input string the result is an empty list).
A 'distinct element' means a distinct character, counted case-insensitively (so 'A' and 'a' count as the same character).
Ascending order, from smallest to largest.
The prefix must be at the start of the string -- i.e. the string must start with the given prefix, not merely contain it anywhere.
The standard mathematical definition: an integer greater than 1 with no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.
No -- the three elements must be distinct elements of the list (three different positions/values), not the same element reused three times.
It means every number in the list -- the function should return True only if ALL numbers in the list are below the threshold, not merely some of them.
Addition: return x + y.

'Properly closed' means every opening bracket '<' has a matching closing bracket '>' later in the string, and at no point does a closing bracket appear before its matching opener (the running count of open brackets never goes negative, and returns to exactly 0 at the end).
'Large prime factor' means the largest prime factor of n -- there is no tie to resolve, since a number's prime factorization is unique and has one well-defined maximum prime factor.
'y' is only treated as a vowel when it is the last character of the word -- not in any other position.

It means every run of 3 consecutive letters in the string must be distinct (i.e. for every window of 3 consecutive characters, no two of those three are the same) -- not that every possible group of any three letters in the string, consecutive or not, must be distinct.

A 'boredom' is specifically a sentence that starts with the word 'I' (as its own word, e.g. 'I am...'), where sentences are delimited by '.', '?', or '!'. It is not about emotional tone or repeated words -- it's this literal starts-with-'I' rule.

A digit is 'even' if its integer value is divisible by 2 (i.e. int(c) % 2 == 0 for that digit character c) -- so 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 are even digits; a number is excluded from the result if it has any even digit.

Not applicable -- the array is guaranteed non-empty per the problem's use case (it contains N integers with N implicitly >= 1); an empty-array right-shift case isn't a scenario the function needs to specially handle beyond the loop naturally doing nothing.

Yes -- there is no limit on the number of exchanged elements between lst1 and lst2, and the exchange is not required to be a strict one-to-one swap; any elements can be moved between the two lists as needed to make all of lst1's elements even.
An 'odd digit' is a digit character with an odd integer value (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), i.e. int(d) % 2 == 1 for that digit character d.

When there is no whitespace and no comma in the text, split on neither -- instead return the count of lowercase letters whose position in the alphabet (ord(c) - ord('a')) is odd, i.e. b, d, f, h, ... (0-indexed odd positions).

'Sorted' means ascending order specifically. A 'duplicate' means an equal adjacent/repeated value; if any number appears more than twice in the list (i.e. more than one duplicate occurrence of the same number), the function should return False even if the list is otherwise in ascending order.

Not applicable -- the problem guarantees the answer is unique (every integer 1..N*N appears exactly once on the grid, and 'it is guaranteed that the answer is unique'), so no tie among multiple minimum paths can occur.

tri(1) = 3; for even n, tri(n) = 1 + n/2; for odd n (other than 1), tri(n) = tri(n-1) + tri(n-2) + tri(n+1). (Note tri(0) = 1 is also needed as a base case for the recursion to bottom out, per the reference implementation's indexing.)

'Closely associated with a word' means the character is immediately adjacent to (part of) an alphabetic sequence -- concretely: the last character is only True if it is alphabetic AND is not immediately preceded by another alphabetic character forming part of the same word (i.e. it must be a single-letter 'word' on its own, isolated by non-letter characters or string boundaries on both sides).

The problem guarantees n is a number to evaluate for this sum property; n is not restricted to only positive values by this function itself, but achieving a sum of exactly 4 positive even numbers requires the total to be a positive even number that is at least 8 -- so non-positive or odd n will simply evaluate as not satisfying that condition (return False), not raise an error.

Only literal space characters ' ' count -- tabs, newlines, and other whitespace are not treated as spaces for this transformation. A run of MORE than 2 consecutive spaces (3 or more) gets replaced entirely with a single '-'; runs of 1 or 2 consecutive spaces are each replaced with underscores (one underscore per space).

An index that is a multiple of both 3 and 4 (i.e. a multiple of 12) is squared, not cubed -- the 'multiple of 3' check takes priority and is checked first, so the cubing rule (which explicitly excludes multiples of 3) never applies to multiples of 12.
Numbers with the same digit sum keep their original relative order from the input list (a stable sort) -- there is no additional secondary sort key specified beyond the digit-sum-ascending order.

A 'triple' is any combination of three indices i, j, k with 1 <= i < j < k <= n (strictly increasing indices, no repeats), and the function counts how many such triples have a[i] + a[j] + a[k] divisible by 3.

Planet order follows their real distance from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (in that order) -- if planet1 is farther from the Sun than planet2, the function still returns the planets strictly between them in this same ascending-distance order (it does not reverse the order based on which argument is farther).
The condition is whether n is a prime number: return x if n is prime, otherwise return y.

A 'valid odd number' means an odd integer (per the standard modulo-2 test) that is not negative -- negative numbers and non-integer values are excluded/ignored entirely, per the explicit rule 'Ignore numbers that are negative or not integers.' Zero and positive integers are evaluated normally for oddness.

'Even digits' means the single even digit values 2, 4, 6, 8 (0 is excluded) that fall within the range bounded by a and b -- the range is effectively clamped to [2, 8] regardless of a/b's actual magnitude, and a/b order doesn't matter (the function takes min/max internally), always returning results in ascending order.
